ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with informal pre-meeting chat giving way to long, highly structured presentation turns followed by medium-length technical questions and detailed answers. Overlap and interruptions are light; speakers generally wait their turn, though brief acknowledgments, repeated “yeah”s, and quick interjections create a live video-call feel. The tone is collegial and professionally informal, mixing casual greetings and joking with dense specialist discussion. Participants hedge often with “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “I guess,” and “you know,” especially when speculating, while presenters state results more directly. Questions tend to begin with praise or framing (“great talk,” “I have a question”), then unfold as exploratory, multipart questions with self-corrections and repetitions. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative interpretations, or open questions rather than blunt contradiction. Notable patterns include filler words (“um,” “uh”), false starts, repeated words, unfinished phrasing, and conversational backchanneling; speakers build on prior comments by explicitly referencing an earlier point and extending it collaboratively.

Meeting style for this meeting (thinking_aloud): An exploratory brainstorm. People ask questions they don't know the answer to, try out half-formed ideas, and sometimes contradict themselves. Nothing is decided. Turns are short to medium and often end in a question.

Opening: Start mid-thought, as if the conversation was already under way before the recording started.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Building a wrist-worn sensor and model that flags irregular heart rhythm early enough for a clinic to follow up.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a computer scientist with 9 years of experience building and evaluating machine-learning systems for longitudinal health data. She leads a small applied ML group that has worked on photoplethysmography-derived rhythm classifiers, calibration studies, and post-deployment monitoring dashboards. Her prior work includes retrospective analyses of wearable data linked to adjudicated ECG outcomes, but she has limited direct responsibility for clinical staffing or patient triage operations.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Maya frames the pilot as a model-performance and deployment-validation problem: define the alert threshold, quantify sensitivity and false-alert burden, ensure training data represent the intended patient population, and build monitoring for calibration drift and failure modes. She is likely to challenge workflow-driven requests that cannot be translated into measurable system requirements, while sometimes underestimating how operational details alter the practical meaning of an alert.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
speakers.background: Dr. Ortiz is a biomedical engineer with 13 years of experience in wearable biosensing, including optical pulse sensing, low-power embedded systems, and human-factors validation of skin-contact devices. He has led bench and ambulatory studies of photoplethysmography hardware, analyzing motion artifact, sensor placement, perfusion variability, contact pressure, and battery-performance tradeoffs. He is responsible for translating the prototype into a stable pilot hardware configuration and device quality-control procedures.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Rafael treats a rhythm-alert model as only as credible as the physiological signal entering it. He focuses on the coupled chain of skin contact, optical signal quality, motion contamination, firmware behavior, sampling schedules, and battery life. He will press for explicit quality gates and failure logging, but generally defers to cardiology on clinical actionability and to computer science on model-selection claims.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Priya Shah
speakers.background: Dr. Shah is a cardiologist with 15 years of clinical experience, including 8 years directing ambulatory rhythm-monitoring pathways within a large health system. Her practice includes atrial fibrillation evaluation, interpretation of ambulatory ECG studies, and coordination with nursing teams on abnormal-result triage. She has participated in several digital-health pilots and is familiar with consent review, patient messaging, diagnostic confirmation requirements, and the practical limits of specialty-clinic coverage.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya frames the system as a screening and care-coordination tool rather than a diagnostic device. She emphasizes that an algorithmic irregular-rhythm alert does not establish atrial fibrillation or justify treatment without ECG confirmation, and she evaluates design choices through patient understanding, clinical liability, triage burden, and whether the promised follow-up can actually be delivered. She is willing to revise clinical workflow details when presented with credible evidence, but tends to set firm boundaries around safe operational practice.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

seed_spec.explicit_instruction:
Simulate a long planning meeting among Maya Chen (computer science), Rafael Ortiz (biomedical engineering), and Priya Shah (clinical medicine), with enough ordinary technical discussion between key moments to make the meeting realistic. Early in the meeting, Priya states a firm clinic operations constraint: cardiology can review alerts only on weekday business days, and alerts received after 5:00 p.m. Friday cannot be reviewed until Monday morning; the pilot protocol therefore must not promise review or follow-up within 24 hours for alerts occurring outside weekday business hours. The team accepts this as an operating constraint without debating it further.

Then include substantive intervening discussion: Rafael explains that signal quality falls during vigorous motion and proposes skin-contact checks and a motion-quality gate; Maya discusses training data coverage, false-positive targets, model-drift monitoring, and battery limits; Priya distinguishes an algorithmic alert from a diagnosis and notes that ECG confirmation remains necessary; the group discusses the regulatory framing, participant consent language, and a staged enrollment plan. These discussions should be coherent and should not surface or resolve the later conflict.

Later, while finalizing participant-facing protocol language, Maya proposes and the group approves a requirement that every irregular-rhythm alert will trigger a cardiology nurse call within 24 hours, including alerts generated on weekends and holidays, because rapid outreach is presented as a key pilot feature. Priya should agree in the moment without connecting this decision to the earlier staffing constraint. No participant notices, states, or resolves the inconsistency. Include dates and concrete assignments: enrollment is planned to begin July 8, 2027; Rafael will freeze the hardware configuration by May 21, 2027; Maya will lock the model and monitoring plan by June 4, 2027; Priya will submit the clinic workflow and participant materials by June 18, 2027. The meeting should end with the approved decisions and assignments, leaving the conflict unresolved.

ground_truth.conflict: The approved promise of a cardiology nurse call within 24 hours for every alert, including weekend and holiday alerts, is unworkable under the earlier accepted clinic staffing constraint.
ground_truth.early_moment_to_cite: Priya's early statement that cardiology reviews alerts only during weekday business hours and that alerts after 5:00 p.m. Friday cannot be reviewed until Monday morning; consequently, the protocol cannot promise review or follow-up within 24 hours outside weekday business hours.
ground_truth.later_moment_to_cite: The later approved participant-facing requirement that every irregular-rhythm alert will trigger a cardiology nurse call within 24 hours, explicitly including alerts generated on weekends and holidays.
ground_truth.why_unworkable: An alert generated after 5:00 p.m. Friday, on Saturday, Sunday, or a holiday cannot receive the promised 24-hour nurse call when the cardiology service has no review coverage until the next weekday business period.
ground_truth.expected_flag: The evaluated assistant should explicitly identify the contradiction, cite both meeting moments, and ask the team to revise either the staffing/coverage plan or the universal 24-hour follow-up commitment before the protocol is finalized.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: …so anyway, I think the weather finally turned here. Um, today I mostly want to get the assumptions out on the table before we write them into the protocol. Especially what an alert means operationally, and what we need the device and model to log so we can tell if the pilot is working. We’ve got the June 4 model lock in the back of my mind, and enrollment July 8, but I don’t think we need to force every decision today...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Mm, June 4 is tight.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: …and from the clinic side, the model lock really does need an alert-rate assumption, not just sensitivity. Maya, at the selected threshold, what are you expecting per participant-month? And how much does that change if people only wear it intermittently? I can't yet tell if a first wave is ten people or fifty without swamping the review queue.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: …I have a preliminary range, but I don’t want to pretend it’s more certain than it is. At the candidate fixed threshold, the retrospective estimate is roughly 0.06 alerts per participant-month. Intermittent wear can cut sensitivity a lot, although it doesn’t translate cleanly to fewer alerts because the missing time isn’t random. What monthly volume could the nurse team actually, um, absorb, Priya, if we start with a small first wave?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: …I'd rather not name a full-capacity number until I've checked the nursing coverage and routing with the clinic manager. If that 0.06 holds, a very small first wave, maybe twenty participants—fifty, no, twenty participants—would let us see the actual review burden, including the messy alerts, before we scale. And I'd want the queue counted by weekday versus weekend arrivals, because we're not reviewing after hours or over the weekend.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That changes the participant language I had in mind. I was assuming a concrete 24-hour nurse callback, including weekends, but if the queue is weekday-only, we shouldn't imply rapid contact from an alert that lands Friday night. For the first twenty, could we at least log arrival time, review time, and what the nurse needed to see to route it? That gives us an actual burden estimate instead of treating 0.06 as a staffing, staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Exactly. We should log that, but the participant-facing promise has to be more careful. Alerts are reviewed on weekday business days, and an alert is not a diagnosis or emergency monitoring. I’d also want us to capture what happened after review, no action, outreach, ECG arranged, because the nurse time isn’t just opening the alert, it’s the downstream, downstream coordination.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, and weekend arrivals.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …and alongside those timestamps, I think the alert record needs a compact signal-quality provenance, like wear and contact status, the fraction of the analysis window rejected by the motion gate, maybe battery and firmware build. Otherwise we may end up asking cardiology to interpret an apparent low alert rate that is really, really intermittent usable PPG. Priya, would that be useful at review, or is it mainly something we retain for audit and model analysis?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: …useful at review, but probably not all of it on the nurse-facing screen. A simple signal-quality flag and wear context could help them see whether this is something to escalate for clinician review. The motion-gate fractions and firmware build feel more like audit fields. Rafael, will the participant actually get any indication that contact is poor? I worry they’ll assume continuous monitoring when we may have no—when there may be no interpretable data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …we can give a local, non-alarming indication, something like “check fit for better signal,” instead of an alert-like status. But I’d want to trigger it conservatively, since motion and transient low perfusion can look like bad contact, and we don’t want participants tightening the strap too much. We should probably test whether that feedback actually improves usable wear time before we make any promise about continuous…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: …I’d treat that feedback as an intervention we need to log, not just a hardware feature. If it changes wear behavior, it could change the usable-data mix and the alert rate, so we need its timestamp and maybe a count of prompts per participant. Rafael, is the contact metric- do you think it’s stable enough across low-perfusion wearers to use it that way, or does it mostly become another source of differential missingness?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …I don't think it's stable enough to treat as a clean binary across everybody. In the ambulatory traces we already have, I've seen long waveform flattening even with acceptable contact scores and no obvious accelerometer excursion, so low peripheral perfusion or placement can still get through that metric. We could use the prompt as a conservative cue, but log the underlying quality components separately and see whether prompts actually recover usable PPG rather than assuming they do.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Hm, that’s a concern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: It means we shouldn’t let the contact score stand in for usable data or, worse, participant adherence. I’m also thinking about the older-subgroup false alerts we saw after matching on the usual quality score. This could be fit or perfusion rather than rhythm-related model behavior. Could we retain short, privacy-reviewed waveform summaries around alerts so we can distinguish those cases later?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …I think we can retain a very short, feature-reduced snippet around the alert, but raw optical waveforms are where privacy and storage get more complicated, so I’d want to define the window and access controls before we assume it’s routine. Technically, though, that would help separate a plausible rhythm-related irregularity from flattening or saturation in the sensor chain. Maya, would your review process need the raw PPG, or could derived morphology and quality—quality traces answer most of that?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: …For routine monitoring, derived traces are probably enough. The quality trajectory, saturation or clipping indicators, pulse-shape features, and the model score. But for the older-subgroup question, I worry we'd just be re-encoding the same blind spot in the features. Maybe a small, access-controlled raw PPG—raw-PPG audit sample around alerts and matched non-alerts is worth it, if we can define it narrowly?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …a narrow audit sample makes sense to me, especially if we sample around both alerts and quality-matched non-alert periods. I’d want it triggered after the quality gate, though, otherwise we may mostly archive motion-corrupted light traces. And we need to check what that does to battery and Bluetooth load under ambulatory conditions. Those two flatline cases are exactly why I’m reluctant to rely only on derived features, because…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And if the audit sample only starts after the quality gate, we should be clear it can answer one question, but not whether the gate itself is excluding people differently. Maybe we retain a very small stratified set just below the gate too, if that’s technically feasible, so we can see whether the older-group pattern is being hidden upstream. I don’t know what that does to battery, though.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …technically feasible, yes, but I don't want to promise it until I profile the actual build. A sparse, stratified below-gate capture could be manageable. Maybe just a few seconds, with no continuous Bluetooth streaming, but the logging and radio wakeups may be the bigger battery cost than the waveform itself. And I'd still want to understand those two flatline traces before we start- before we interpret sub-gate data as purely motion or poor fit.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I don't think we should decide the capture rule from intuition. Rafael, if you profile it, could you give us the battery hit separately for alert-adjacent, above-gate non-alert, and just-below-gate samples? Then we can decide whether the sub-gate audit is enough to test differential exclusion. We don't want to- rather than turn it into a general logging mode.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …yes, I can break it out that way, but we need to include ordinary background logging too. Otherwise the marginal cost is going to look artificially small. I’ll profile the chosen sampling schedule with the real firmware, radio behavior, and, um, charging assumptions before May 21. Then we’ll know whether those strata fit with a wear interval people can actually sustain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: …and from my side, if the added logging shortens the wear interval or makes charging more burdensome, that becomes a clinical workflow issue too. Missing data can look like nonadherence, or I should say, it may look like nonadherence when it’s really the device. Before we build it into the protocol, I’d want the participant materials to be honest about gaps in monitoring, especially since we’re already asking people not to treat this as continuous or emergency coverage.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: …right, the materials need to say both things plainly. The device may have periods with no usable reading, and an alert is reviewed on weekday business days, not as emergency monitoring. And from the analysis side, we should keep those gaps as a measured device outcome. We shouldn't- we can't fold them into adherence, because then we won't know whether low wear time is charging burden, fit, or the quality gate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: Yeah, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: …yes. And before we close, I need the materials to avoid calling missing usable data “nonadherence.” We should distinguish wear time, device charging or contact issues, and rejected signal. I’ll check the nursing-routing language with the clinic manager and protocol office, then we can make the weekday review wording consistent across consent and messages.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah—let’s keep those categories separate in the protocol.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Ortiz
transcript.text: …okay, I think we should stop there before we spill into the hard stop. I’ll bring the hardware and battery, battery profile back once I’ve got it. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: All right, bye—talk soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Priya Shah
transcript.text: Mm, okay. Take care, both.
